# Built-in browser

The built-in browser is a real browser pane inside the Codex desktop app, separate from the person's Chrome. Its tools are named `mcp__Claude_Browser__*` when the session itself runs inside the desktop app, and `mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__*` when the session runs in the cloud (started from the web, a phone, or the desktop app) and is linked to the person's computer. The names after the prefix are the same either way, Codex uses whichever prefix is actually present, and this skill refers to the tools by the part after the prefix.

If the only built-in browser tool present is `enable__mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser`, Codex calls it first: it turns the built-in browser on for this conversation, and the `mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__*` tools appear once it has run.

## What the person can see

The browser pane shares the desktop app's side panel with artifacts, documents, and file previews, and the panel shows one of them at a time. While the browser pane is showing, the person sees what Codex sees and can browse or take over at any time. While something else is open in the panel, or the panel is closed, the built-in browser keeps working but the person cannot see it.

Right before asking the person to do something in the built-in browser themselves (click a button, sign in, complete a verification step), Codex calls `tabs_context`, whose result ends by saying whether the Browser pane is displayed, hidden, or not open. If the pane is not open, Codex opens the page first and checks again. If the pane is hidden, Codex first asks the person to bring the browser back in the Codex desktop app: press Cmd+Shift+B on Mac or Ctrl+Shift+B on Windows, or close whatever else is open in the side panel and click the globe icon (the Browser button). Codex then says what to do in the browser. Codex asks because using the browser does not bring the pane back, and what the panel shows is the person's choice. Codex also says in the conversation what it found or did in the browser, because the person may not have been watching the pane.

## Sign-ins persist, and they are the person's

The built-in browser keeps its own persistent profile, shared across the desktop app's sessions. The person, or an earlier session, may already be signed in to sites there, and sign-ins Codex completes persist for later. Codex treats existing sessions as the person's: it never signs out, changes credentials, or acts on an account beyond what the task needs.

## Tabs

The built-in browser has tabs. `preview_start` with a `url` opens an additional tab at that URL in one call and returns a `tabId`, leaving existing tabs untouched, so Codex prefers it over `tabs_create` followed by `navigate` when the destination is already known. `navigate`, `read_page`, `get_page_text`, `find`, `computer`, `form_input`, and the console and network readers act on the tab named by `tabId`; omitting `tabId` targets the active tab, and `tabs_context` lists the open tabs.

## Loading via ToolSearch

Codex loads the built-in browser tools in bulk, not one-by-one: if they are in the deferred list, Codex loads them all in a single ToolSearch call whose query is their full name prefix, for example `{ query: "mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__", max_results: 64 }`.

## Reading pages

Codex prefers `get_page_text` and `read_page` over screenshots for reading, because they return the page's actual text and structure rather than pixels of the visible viewport. `computer` with action "screenshot" is for when the visual layout is the point or the person asks to see the page.

## Site approvals, blocked sites, and request_access

Depending on the person's approval settings, the person may be asked to approve a site before Codex acts on it, and some sites are blocked outright. Codex waits for a pending approval rather than working around it. If a page is refused or an approval is declined, Codex tells the person and moves on rather than retrying.

When the tools carry the `mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__` prefix, approvals can be answered from any of the person's devices and may take a moment to arrive, and the session may also have a `request_access` tool. If a browser tool answers that the site is not allowed yet and `request_access` is present, Codex calls it with that site's URL and scope "once" (or "site" when the task will keep using that site), waits for the person's answer, and then retries the original tool. Without `request_access`, a refused site is handled as above: Codex tells the person and moves on.

## What the built-in browser cannot open

The built-in browser cannot open `file://` URLs or `localhost` servers that Codex starts itself, because those run where Codex's shell runs, which is not where the browser pane runs. To show the person HTML that Codex generated, Codex uses an artifact instead.

## When the built-in browser cannot be reached

When the tools carry the `mcp__remote-devices__Claude_Browser__` prefix, the pane runs in the Codex desktop app on the person's computer while Codex runs elsewhere, so it is reachable only while that app is open and online. If those tool calls cannot reach the desktop app (connection errors or no response), Codex tells the person the built-in browser looks offline on their computer rather than retrying, and follows the session's browser guidance on whether to continue with the other browser or ask first.

# Museum tour visitor experience proposal

## Visitor verdict

## How much information belongs at a stop?

## Priorities

## How to judge the changes

# Under the skin — a visitor’s review

**8/10 as a museum companion.** At the 300 SL, I could see the open doors in the photograph, cut down the frame for conventional doors, and watch it twist. That experiment gives me a reason to look back at the real car. The harder part is finding the right stop from the gallery floor and knowing which of the moving numbers deserves my attention.

I would fund two changes first. Give visitors a shortcut to the room they are standing in, and put each mechanism’s most revealing experiment beside its first control. The tour already has enough exhibits and engineering detail.

| Part of the visit | Rating | What earns or costs points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Recognizing the car and finding its stop | 6/10 | All 46 stops have a photo, and the cards are grouped by room. On a 393 × 659 phone viewport, Legend 6 began about 32 screen heights down the index. Looking for “Gullwing” in the English card text found the SLS AMG and missed the 300 SL. |
| Learning from the exhibit | 9/10 | The pinned model stays visible while I change the frame or open the SLK roof. I can test a prediction and see the answer. On the Gullwing, the paragraph connecting the frame to the doors was below the visible screen after I tapped the comparison. |
| Choosing how deeply to explore | 7/10 | One mechanism is enough for a satisfying stop, and 34 of the 46 stops have just one. Even a single mechanism can present controls, units, a legend and several facts before I know what to watch. |
| Using the tour between galleries | 9/10 | English and Hungarian, named previous/next links and offline access make it practical to carry. After “Ready offline” appeared, I disconnected Chromium and opened a previously unvisited Evolution II stop. Its model animated. |

## What to change first

1. **Give the index two useful shortcuts.** Keep “See the route.” Add “Three highlights” beside it, linking to the existing three-car tour, and a return link from the highlights to the full route. At the start of the route, add “Jump to a room” using the 11 existing room headings and their levels. Native fragment links can do the work. Include familiar names such as “300 SL Gullwing” in card text so the browser’s Find command works too. A visitor arriving at Level 3 should be able to go straight to Legend 6 and still see the photo cards that help identify the car. [Route page](../index.html) · [Room order](../stops/tour.js) · [Highlights](../teaser.html)

2. **Edit each stop around one observation and one experiment.** Pilot this on the Gullwing and SLK. Keep the best instruction and the readout that answers it together. Put secondary measurements and the remaining technical facts in a native disclosure with a specific title, such as “Frame loads and stiffness.” Keep the controls, units and any qualification needed to interpret the visible result in view. [Gullwing story](../stops/300sl/car.js) · [SLK story](../stops/slk/car.js)

   For the **Gullwing**, the phone could say, “Look at the high sill beneath the open door. Tap ‘Cut down for normal doors’ and watch the frame twist.” Beside the comparison, explain “In this simplified model, lowering the sides leaves about a third of the original stiffness.” The existing control produced 35% in the walkthrough. Someone who wants the tube forces can open the detail. Someone who looks up from the screen already knows why the doors open upwards.

   For the **SLK**, the existing “Open the roof” button is already a good invitation. Bring the observation “Watch which moves first, the boot lid or the roof” beside it. The phase indicator gives the answer. The three angle readouts can sit one tap deeper. This change can shorten the reading path simply by moving existing material.

3. **Make the first photograph useful immediately.** The shared story currently creates a hidden image and reveals it after the 3D viewer initializes. A rendering failure can therefore leave someone standing at the car with an error message and the identifying photo hidden. Show the existing photo, its credit and the takeaway as soon as the story appears. Keep them readable if 3D fails. Also change the index invitation to “Scroll to see where the mechanism sits” so it describes the gesture the tour actually uses. [Viewer](../lib/app/viewer.js) · [Story layout](../lib/app/story.js)

## What information is missing?

**For a short visit, the missing information is where to look.** Across the tour, 59 component stories already contain 229 technical talking points. The opening question, one visible feature of the real exhibit, and the consequence for its driver or passenger have more value on the first screen than another specification. Keep generous depth for enthusiasts, especially the comparisons, sources and clearly identified model assumptions.

**For finding a car, visitors need to know how closely the photo and location match.** The SLK already has a photo, but it shows a street car in Washington, D.C. That explanation comes in the background, after the interaction. Put “Reference photo of the same generation” beside the image. For uncertain rooms, put a brief qualifier next to the room name until someone has checked the exhibit on site. Start with Collection 4 and the 220 S. A gallery check here is worth more than drawing a precise floor map from uncertain locations. [SLK photo note](../stops/slk/car.js) · [Open location questions](../AGENTS.md)

## How to decide whether the changes work

- **Try the pilot on the floor.** Ask five first-time visitors to find a car from its room sign, choose a short visit from the home page, then use the Gullwing comparison and explain the door shape in their own words. A proposed pass is four of five completing each task unaided. Watch where they look back at the car and whether anyone who wants the figures can still find them.
- **Compare on the same phone before and after.** On a physical iPhone, repeat cold opens of the route and the Gullwing under the same network conditions. Record time to usable route links, first visible photo and first working control. Compare frame times while orbiting and changing a control on the Blitzen-Benz wind tunnel. Recheck on iPad and with reduced motion, VoiceOver and Hungarian labels. Investigate any repeatable slowdown before rollout.
- **Protect offline use.** The reviewed build packaged about 9.7 MiB of uncompressed assets. The proposed shortcuts and copy can reuse the current photos and models, add zero new media requests, and keep 3D off the index’s rendering path. After “Ready offline,” repeat the room jump, highlights link and an unseen stop in airplane mode. The existing offline test is a starting point. [Build](../tools/build.mjs) · [Offline test](../tests/e2e/offline.spec.mjs)

*Review basis, 18 November 2026.* I reviewed the route and content inventory at revision `59b1e58`, walked the index, Gullwing comparison, SLK roof control, language switch and highlights in iPhone-sized WebKit, and checked offline entry in Chromium. The ratings are editorial judgments. Actual gallery locations, visitor comprehension and physical-device timing still need field checks.

# Under the skin — a visitor’s review

**8/10 as a museum companion.** At the 300 SL, I could see the open doors in the photograph, cut down the frame for conventional doors, and watch it twist. That experiment gives me a reason to look back at the real car. The harder part is finding the right stop from the gallery floor and knowing which of the moving numbers deserves my attention.

I would fund two changes first. Give visitors a shortcut to the room they are standing in, and put each mechanism’s most revealing experiment beside its first control. The tour already has enough exhibits and engineering detail.

| Part of the visit | Rating | What earns or costs points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Recognizing the car and finding its stop | 6/10 | All 46 stops have a photo, and the cards are grouped by room. On a 393 × 659 phone viewport, Legend 6 began about 32 screen heights down the index. Looking for “Gullwing” in the English card text found the SLS AMG and missed the 300 SL. |
| Learning from the exhibit | 9/10 | The pinned model stays visible while I change the frame or open the SLK roof. I can test a prediction and see the answer. On the Gullwing, the paragraph connecting the frame to the doors was below the visible screen after I tapped the comparison. |
| Choosing how deeply to explore | 7/10 | One mechanism is enough for a satisfying stop, and 34 of the 46 stops have just one. Even a single mechanism can present controls, units, a legend and several facts before I know what to watch. |
| Using the tour between galleries | 9/10 | English and Hungarian, named previous/next links and offline access make it practical to carry. After “Ready offline” appeared, I disconnected Chromium and opened a previously unvisited Evolution II stop. Its model animated. |

## What to change first

1. **Give the index two useful shortcuts.** Keep “See the route.” Add “Three highlights” beside it, linking to the existing three-car tour, and a return link from the highlights to the full route. At the start of the route, add “Jump to a room” using the 11 existing room headings and their levels. Native fragment links can do the work. Include familiar names such as “300 SL Gullwing” in card text so the browser’s Find command works too. A visitor arriving at Level 3 should be able to go straight to Legend 6 and still see the photo cards that help identify the car. [Route page](../index.html) · [Room order](../stops/tour.js) · [Highlights](../teaser.html)

2. **Edit each stop around one observation and one experiment.** Pilot this on the Gullwing and SLK. Keep the best instruction and the readout that answers it together. Put secondary measurements and the remaining technical facts in a native disclosure with a specific title, such as “Frame loads and stiffness.” Keep the controls, units and any qualification needed to interpret the visible result in view. [Gullwing story](../stops/300sl/car.js) · [SLK story](../stops/slk/car.js)

   For the **Gullwing**, the phone could say, “Look at the high sill beneath the open door. Tap ‘Cut down for normal doors’ and watch the frame twist.” Beside the comparison, explain “In this simplified model, lowering the sides leaves about a third of the original stiffness.” The existing control produced 35% in the walkthrough. Someone who wants the tube forces can open the detail. Someone who looks up from the screen already knows why the doors open upwards.

   For the **SLK**, the existing “Open the roof” button is already a good invitation. Bring the observation “Watch which moves first, the boot lid or the roof” beside it. The phase indicator gives the answer. The three angle readouts can sit one tap deeper. This change can shorten the reading path simply by moving existing material.

3. **Make the first photograph useful immediately.** The shared story currently creates a hidden image and reveals it after the 3D viewer initializes. A rendering failure can therefore leave someone standing at the car with an error message and the identifying photo hidden. Show the existing photo, its credit and the takeaway as soon as the story appears. Keep them readable if 3D fails. Also change the index invitation to “Scroll to see where the mechanism sits” so it describes the gesture the tour actually uses. [Viewer](../lib/app/viewer.js) · [Story layout](../lib/app/story.js)

## What information is missing?

**For a short visit, the missing information is where to look.** Across the tour, 59 component stories already contain 229 technical talking points. The opening question, one visible feature of the real exhibit, and the consequence for its driver or passenger have more value on the first screen than another specification. Keep generous depth for enthusiasts, especially the comparisons, sources and clearly identified model assumptions.

**For finding a car, visitors need to know how closely the photo and location match.** The SLK already has a photo, but it shows a street car in Washington, D.C. That explanation comes in the background, after the interaction. Put “Reference photo of the same generation” beside the image. For uncertain rooms, put a brief qualifier next to the room name until someone has checked the exhibit on site. Start with Collection 4 and the 220 S. A gallery check here is worth more than drawing a precise floor map from uncertain locations. [SLK photo note](../stops/slk/car.js) · [Open location questions](../AGENTS.md)

## How to decide whether the changes work

- **Try the pilot on the floor.** Ask five first-time visitors to find a car from its room sign, choose a short visit from the home page, then use the Gullwing comparison and explain the door shape in their own words. A proposed pass is four of five completing each task unaided. Watch where they look back at the car and whether anyone who wants the figures can still find them.
- **Compare on the same phone before and after.** On a physical iPhone, repeat cold opens of the route and the Gullwing under the same network conditions. Record time to usable route links, first visible photo and first working control. Compare frame times while orbiting and changing a control on the Blitzen-Benz wind tunnel. Recheck on iPad and with reduced motion, VoiceOver and Hungarian labels. Investigate any repeatable slowdown before rollout.
- **Protect offline use.** The reviewed build packaged about 9.7 MiB of uncompressed assets. The proposed shortcuts and copy can reuse the current photos and models, add zero new media requests, and keep 3D off the index’s rendering path. After “Ready offline,” repeat the room jump, highlights link and an unseen stop in airplane mode. The existing offline test is a starting point. [Build](../tools/build.mjs) · [Offline test](../tests/e2e/offline.spec.mjs)

*Review basis, 18 November 2026.* I reviewed the route and content inventory at revision `59b1e58`, walked the index, Gullwing comparison, SLK roof control, language switch and highlights in iPhone-sized WebKit, and checked offline entry in Chromium. The ratings are editorial judgments. Actual gallery locations, visitor comprehension and physical-device timing still need field checks.

The recommendation is to give each car **one question worth stopping for**. The route card asks it, the photo shows where to look, and the first control lets the visitor discover the answer. Keep that control, its result and a plain-language explanation together. Group the deeper measurements under a title that tells visitors what they’ll learn by opening it.

The proposal works through three distinct flows:

- **SLK:** Ask which moves first, the boot lid or the roof. Put “Open the roof” beside the phase indicator, then connect the folded roof to the luggage space it occupies.
- **300 SL Gullwing:** Start at the high sill and let visitors see why lowering it weakens the frame. The low bonnet then introduces a second question about how the six-cylinder engine fits underneath.
- **540 K:** Tell the three mechanisms as one drive. Cross a bump to see the suspension work, floor the pedal to engage the supercharger, then compare two body shapes at the same power.

These three cars make a useful pilot because they cover one-, two- and three-mechanism stops using the tour’s existing photos, controls and models.
